questions.question: Post-amendment, an open-ended restricted scheme may invest in unlisted securities only:
questions.option_A: After obtaining specific IFSCA approval for each unlisted investment
questions.option_B: After 12 months of operations
questions.option_C: Upon achieving the minimum corpus of USD 3 Million
questions.option_D: If unlisted exposure stays below 50% of corpus
questions.correct_text: Upon achieving the minimum corpus of USD 3 Million
questions.explanation: New proviso inserted in Reg. 35(1) by the 2026 Amendment: unlisted-securities investments by an open-ended scheme may be undertaken only upon achieving the USD 3 Million minimum corpus. The pre-existing 25%-of-corpus cap on unlisted securities continues to apply on top of this gating condition.

questions.question: An open-ended restricted scheme may commence investment activities upon raising:
questions.option_A: USD 3 Million — that is, the full minimum corpus, before any investment activity begins
questions.option_B: USD 500,000, with no further corpus milestone applying to the scheme at any stage
questions.option_C: Any amount at all, provided that at least twenty investors have subscribed to it
questions.option_D: USD 1 Million, with the USD 3 Million minimum corpus achieved within 12 months of the PPM being taken on record
questions.correct_text: USD 1 Million, with the USD 3 Million minimum corpus achieved within 12 months of the PPM being taken on record
questions.explanation: Reg. 35(2) proviso: commence at USD 1 Million; achieve USD 3 Million within 12 months from the taken-on-record communication. Read with the new Reg. 35(1) proviso: until USD 3 Million is achieved, that open-ended scheme cannot deploy into unlisted securities.

questions.question: The January 2026 Amendment inserted a new ground for winding up a scheme. It applies where:
questions.option_A: The FME raised funds but missed the minimum corpus within the (extended) PPM validity, and did not extend that validity by filing and paying the fee
questions.option_B: The Authority, acting suo motu, determines that the scheme has become unviable and directs that it be wound up
questions.option_C: Investors holding fifty per cent of the value of the scheme pass a resolution requiring it to be wound up
questions.option_D: The net asset value of the scheme falls fifty per cent below par and the FME cannot restore it that year
questions.correct_text: The FME raised funds but missed the minimum corpus within the (extended) PPM validity, and did not extend that validity by filing and paying the fee
questions.explanation: New Reg. 131(1)(c): an exit route where a scheme raised some money, never hit minimum corpus within validity, and the FME has not filed (with fee) for a further extension. The 2026 Amendment ALSO inserted Reg. 131(1)(d): winding up where no investors were onboarded and no funds collected, and the FME voluntarily desires to wind up. The 75%-by-value investor resolution under Reg. 131(1)(b) remains separate again.

questions.question: A retail scheme required to appoint an IFSC-based custodian may, under the substituted Explanation II, make that appointment within:
questions.option_A: Twelve (12) months from the launch of the scheme, using any independent custodian meanwhile
questions.option_B: 24 months from commencement of the 2026 Amendment, using an India/foreign-regulated custodian in the interim
questions.option_C: No transition at all — an IFSC-based custodian is required from the very first day
questions.option_D: Six (6) months from the filing of the placement memorandum with the Authority itself
questions.correct_text: 24 months from commencement of the 2026 Amendment, using an India/foreign-regulated custodian in the interim
questions.explanation: 24-month runway from 30.01.2026. During the window, the FME may appoint an independent custodian in India or any foreign jurisdiction regulated by the local financial sector regulator, with information arrangements for IFSCA. Anchor fact alongside it: Reg. 132 mandates custodians for retail schemes, open-ended restricted schemes, and all other schemes with AUM above USD 70 Million.

questions.question: A Registered FME wants to manage schemes on behalf of a foreign asset manager (a "third-party"). It must:
questions.option_A: Simply disclose the arrangement in the placement memorandum of every scheme
questions.option_B: Obtain a fresh FME registration under a new category created for the purpose
questions.option_C: Seek authorisation from IFSCA under Part D of Chapter [on third-party fund management services]
questions.option_D: Route the whole arrangement through a co-investment special purpose vehicle
questions.correct_text: Seek authorisation from IFSCA under Part D of Chapter [on third-party fund management services]
questions.explanation: Part D (Reg. 107A–107D), inserted by the July 2025 Amendment (w.e.f. 30.07.2025), created a dedicated authorisation regime. A "third-party fund manager" must itself be registered/regulated for fund management or similar activity with the financial sector regulator of its country of incorporation. The FME may continue its own schemes and PMS in parallel under its existing registration.

questions.question: In a third-party fund management arrangement, if the third-party indemnifies the FME fully, the FME's regulatory liability for the schemes:
questions.option_A: Transfers to the third-party manager to the full extent of the indemnity given
questions.option_B: Is shared proportionately between them in the manner set out in the arrangement
questions.option_C: Ceases once the Authority has approved the third-party arrangement in writing
questions.option_D: Continues in full — the FME remains liable notwithstanding any indemnification arrangement
questions.correct_text: Continues in full — the FME remains liable notwithstanding any indemnification arrangement
questions.explanation: Reg. 107C(4) is explicit: notwithstanding any arrangement with the third-party, including indemnification, the FME continues to be liable for all obligations arising from the arrangement. Indemnities are a commercial recovery mechanism inter se — they never dilute regulatory accountability. The FME must also strengthen compliance resources commensurate to scale (Reg. 107C(2)).

questions.question: An FME seeking authorisation for third-party fund management services must be set up in IFSC as:
questions.option_A: A company, LLP, or any other form permitted by the Authority
questions.option_B: A company only, and no other legal form is permitted at all
questions.option_C: A trust having an IFSC-based trustee appointed to it
questions.option_D: A branch of the foreign third-party manager concerned
questions.correct_text: A company, LLP, or any other form permitted by the Authority
questions.explanation: Reg. 107D(1): company, LLP, or any other form as may be permitted by the Authority. A branch structure would sit oddly with the liability architecture of Reg. 107C(4), which presumes a substantively resourced IFSC entity.

questions.question: Post-amendment, an individual with post-qualification experience of 2 years in an eligible institution plus Authority-specified certifications is eligible as:
questions.option_A: Any KMP of the FME
questions.option_B: The KMP referred under sub-regulation (2) only
questions.option_C: Principal Officer only
questions.option_D: No KMP role — 5 years is an absolute floor
questions.correct_text: The KMP referred under sub-regulation (2) only
questions.explanation: The 2-year + certification route applies only to the KMP under sub-regulation (2). For KMPs under sub-regulations (1), (3) and (4), the certification route requires 3 years' post-qualification experience. Separately, a professional qualification (CA/CS/CMA-type membership) reduces the clause (b) experience requirement to 3 years for the sub-regulation (2) KMP. Three distinct relaxation tracks — map them precisely.

questions.question: The 25% / 50% extension fees are computed on:
questions.option_A: The filing fee that the FME actually paid when the scheme was originally filed
questions.option_B: The corpus of the scheme raised up to the date of the extension application
questions.option_C: The applicable fee for filing a fresh scheme, as prevalent at the time of the extension
questions.option_D: A flat amount in USD notified by the Authority at the start of every year
questions.correct_text: The applicable fee for filing a fresh scheme, as prevalent at the time of the extension
questions.explanation: The amended provisos peg the fee to the fresh-scheme filing fee "as may be prevalent at the time of such extension" — a floating base. If IFSCA revises its fee schedule between original filing and extension, the revised fee applies. Drafting detail, but exactly the kind examiners isolate.

questions.source: IFSCA (Fund Management) (Amendment) Regulations, 2026 / IFSCA (Fund Management) (Amendment) Regulations, 2025

questions.source: 29th IFSCA Authority Meeting, 24 July 2026 (approved; not yet notified)
questions.question: Today, an FME's contribution to its own VC scheme is capped at what share of targeted corpus?
questions.option_A: 25%, effective from the date of the Authority meeting held on 24 July 2026
questions.option_B: 2.5%, which operates as both the floor and the ceiling for such schemes
questions.option_C: There is no ceiling at all on an FME's contribution to a VC scheme
questions.option_D: 10% — the notified ceiling under Reg. 28(1); the approved 25% is not yet notified
questions.correct_text: 10% — the notified ceiling under Reg. 28(1); the approved 25% is not yet notified
questions.explanation: Reg. 28(1) caps the contribution at 10% of targeted corpus, and that is what binds until the amendment is notified. Two separate things are easily confused: (i) the ALREADY-notified carve-out disapplying the 10% ceiling where the FME and its associates are resident outside India with no Indian UBO and not more than one-third of corpus goes to one investee; and (ii) the APPROVED 25% ceiling for FMEs with Indian UBOs investing only in IFSC/foreign jurisdictions. 2.5% is the floor, not the ceiling.

questions.source: 29th IFSCA Authority Meeting, 24 July 2026 (approved; not yet notified)
questions.question: As the law stands today, the scheme Annual Report must reach the Authority within:
questions.option_A: Four months — Reg. 134; the six-month extension is approved but not yet notified
questions.option_B: Three months from the end of the financial year of the scheme concerned
questions.option_C: Six months, per the approval granted at the July 2026 Authority meeting
questions.option_D: Twelve months from the end of the financial year of the scheme concerned
questions.correct_text: Four months — Reg. 134; the six-month extension is approved but not yet notified
questions.explanation: Reg. 134(1): not later than four months from the end of the financial year, with the abridged summary to investors on the same four-month clock (Reg. 134(3)) and the full report within 15 days of an investor's request. The extension to six months was approved on 24 July 2026 but is not yet notified — diarise four months, plan for six.

questions.source: 29th IFSCA Authority Meeting, 24 July 2026 (approved; not yet notified)
questions.question: Under the approved framework for differential distribution, the minimum investment in junior / subordinate classes of units will be:
questions.option_A: USD 150,000 for every investor, whatever the class of units subscribed for
questions.option_B: USD 1 Million from non-individual Accredited Investors, or USD 2 Million from other investors
questions.option_C: USD 250,000, matching the minimum applicable to a venture capital scheme
questions.option_D: There is no minimum at all prescribed for junior or subordinate classes
questions.correct_text: USD 1 Million from non-individual Accredited Investors, or USD 2 Million from other investors
questions.explanation: The approved Regulatory Framework sets USD 1 Million for non-individual Accredited Investors and USD 2 Million for other investors in junior/subordinate classes — higher thresholds because those units may absorb losses ahead of senior capital. ESG Schemes may additionally accept grants, subject to conditions. The PPM must prominently disclose the classes, distribution rights and risks.

questions.source: 29th IFSCA Authority Meeting, 24 July 2026 (approved; not yet notified)
questions.question: An amendment has been approved at an IFSCA Authority meeting but not yet notified in the Gazette. Which position must the FME comply with?
questions.option_A: The approved position, from the date of the Authority meeting
questions.option_B: Either position, at the FME's discretion, if disclosed in the PPM
questions.option_C: The existing notified regulations — until the amendment is notified
questions.option_D: Nothing changes until IFSCA separately issues a circular permitting reliance
questions.correct_text: The existing notified regulations — until the amendment is notified
questions.explanation: Compliance is owed to the notified text. An Authority approval signals a coming change and is essential for planning, but it does not displace the regulation in force — acting early is a breach, and several approved easements carry their own conditions (for example the NAV change requires 75%-by-value investor approval), so they are not self-executing even after notification.

questions.option_A: None at all — the Authority has approved all three of the changes in question already

questions.option_C: Two — the contribution ceiling and the annual report date, but not the NAV periodicity
