questions.question: Approved & Coming — Flash Deck
A Registered FME (Non-Retail) is asked to act as investment manager for a REIT proposing a public offer. Which statement is MOST accurate?
questions.option_A: It may act only for private placements; a public offer requires Registered FME (Retail)
questions.option_B: It may act, since a Non-Retail FME is permitted to manage REITs and InvITs generally
questions.option_C: It may act if the REIT's units will be listed on a recognised stock exchange in the IFSC
questions.option_D: It may act provided it maintains net worth of USD 1,000,000 for that mandate alone
questions.correct_text: It may act only for private placements; a public offer requires Registered FME (Retail)
questions.explanation: Reg. 4(b) permits a Non-Retail FME to act as investment manager for PRIVATE PLACEMENTS of REITs and InvITs. Public offers sit exclusively with a Registered FME (Retail) under Reg. 4(c). Listing status and a mandate-specific net worth are not the operative tests — the category is.

questions.question: A Registered FME (Non-Retail) met USD 500,000 net worth at registration. Eighteen months later accumulated losses reduce it to USD 460,000. What should the compliance officer identify first?
questions.option_A: That net worth is an entry condition, tested only at the time of registration
questions.option_B: That net worth must be maintained at all times, so the FME is currently in breach
questions.option_C: That the shortfall is acceptable while the FME remains profitable on a cash basis
questions.option_D: That the FME may continue provided it restores the shortfall before the year end
questions.correct_text: That net worth must be maintained at all times, so the FME is currently in breach
questions.explanation: Reg. 8(1) requires the net worth to be maintained at ALL times. It is a continuing obligation, not an entry gate, so the breach exists now — the question of how quickly it is cured comes second.

questions.question: A branch FME's parent holds net worth far above the prescribed minimum, but none of it is earmarked for the IFSC branch. What is the position?
questions.option_A: Compliant, because the requirement attaches to the parent's total net worth
questions.option_B: Compliant, provided the parent furnishes an annual solvency certificate
questions.option_C: Not compliant, because the amount must be earmarked for the branch in the IFSC
questions.option_D: Not compliant, because a branch must hold the net worth within the IFSC itself
questions.correct_text: Not compliant, because the amount must be earmarked for the branch in the IFSC
questions.explanation: Reg. 8(2) permits the minimum net worth to sit at parent level, but its proviso requires that amount to be EARMARKED for the IFSC branch. Holding a large balance sheet generally is not enough; equally, the regulation does not require the funds to be held inside the IFSC.

questions.question: Which activity can an Authorised FME undertake WITHOUT moving to a higher category?
questions.option_A: Offering Portfolio Management Services to accredited investors
questions.option_B: Launching a restricted scheme open to accredited investors
questions.option_C: Acting as investment manager for a private placement of an InvIT
questions.option_D: Managing a Family Investment Fund established for a Single Family
questions.correct_text: Managing a Family Investment Fund established for a Single Family
questions.explanation: Reg. 4(a) confines an Authorised FME to Venture Capital Schemes for accredited/threshold investors and a Family Investment Fund for a Single Family. Portfolio Management Services, restricted schemes and private placements of REITs/InvITs all require Registered FME (Non-Retail).

questions.question: An Authorised FME intends to begin offering Portfolio Management Services next quarter. What should the compliance officer examine FIRST?
questions.option_A: Whether PMS falls within the activities permitted to its present category
questions.option_B: Whether the proposed clients qualify as accredited investors under the rules
questions.option_C: Whether the FME's net worth exceeds USD 500,000 on its latest balance sheet
questions.option_D: Whether the principal officer holds the experience prescribed for such mandates
questions.correct_text: Whether PMS falls within the activities permitted to its present category
questions.explanation: All four matter eventually, but scope comes first: PMS is not open to an Authorised FME under Reg. 4(a). Without a category change under Reg. 13(2) — which needs the Authority's prior approval — the investor, net worth and personnel questions never arise.

questions.question: A candidate KMP holds a professional qualification and four years' relevant experience. For a role under sub-regulation (2), the compliance officer should conclude that the candidate:
questions.option_A: Qualifies, because the professional-qualification route reduces the requirement to three years
questions.option_B: Falls short, because the base requirement of five years applies to every KMP role
questions.option_C: Qualifies only after obtaining the certification prescribed by the Authority as well
questions.option_D: Falls short, because professional qualifications count only towards the certification route
questions.correct_text: Qualifies, because the professional-qualification route reduces the requirement to three years
questions.explanation: The first proviso to Reg. 7(5)(b) reduces the requirement to three years where the KMP holds a professional qualification. Four years therefore suffices. The five-year figure is the base rule, and the certification route is a separate alternative rather than an additional condition.

questions.question: An FME registered in the IFSC also carries on a separate regulated activity outside the IFSC for which it maintains net worth. On the FME net worth requirement, the correct view is that it:
questions.option_A: May be met by the same net worth, provided the aggregate exceeds both thresholds
questions.option_B: Must be met separately, being additional to net worth held for any other activity
questions.option_C: May be met by the parent, provided the parent is regulated in its home jurisdiction
questions.option_D: Must be met separately only where the other activity is carried on within the IFSC
questions.correct_text: Must be met separately, being additional to net worth held for any other activity
questions.explanation: Reg. 8(3) makes the FME requirement separate from and in addition to net worth required for other activities, whether inside or outside the IFSC. Double-counting the same capital is the error the provision exists to prevent.

questions.question: An FME proposes that its Principal Officer also act as Compliance Officer to keep headcount lean. The compliance risk here is that:
questions.option_A: The Principal Officer must be resident in India while the Compliance Officer need not be
questions.option_B: The Authority requires a minimum of four key managerial personnel in every registered FME
questions.option_C: The roles carry distinct responsibilities and the Compliance Officer reports to the board
questions.option_D: The Principal Officer is responsible only for fund management, not for compliance oversight
questions.correct_text: The roles carry distinct responsibilities and the Compliance Officer reports to the board
questions.explanation: The Principal Officer carries overall responsibility for the FME's activities, while the Compliance Officer reports to the board (or the head of the organisation). Collapsing the roles removes the independent reporting line that the structure is designed to create.

questions.question: A venture capital scheme has 48 investors and wishes to admit 4 more, each investing USD 300,000. The compliance officer should identify that:
questions.option_A: The additional investors are permissible because each exceeds the USD 250,000 minimum
questions.option_B: The scheme may admit them only after converting into a restricted scheme structure
questions.option_C: The ceiling applies to accredited investors only, so the admissions are unaffected
questions.option_D: Admitting all four would breach the fifty-investor ceiling applicable to VC schemes
questions.correct_text: Admitting all four would breach the fifty-investor ceiling applicable to VC schemes
questions.explanation: The ticket size is satisfied, but the investor ceiling for a VC scheme is fifty. Admitting four more would take the scheme to fifty-two. Meeting one condition does not cure a breach of another — the classic error in scheme structuring.

questions.question: A VC scheme's placement memorandum is silent on leverage, but the FME wishes to borrow short-term to bridge a drawdown. The correct position is that borrowing:
questions.option_A: Requires the maximum leverage and its calculation methodology to be disclosed in the PPM
questions.option_B: Is prohibited outright, since venture capital schemes may never employ leverage
questions.option_C: Is permitted, because bridge borrowing against committed capital is always excluded
questions.option_D: Requires the prior approval of the Authority for each individual borrowing transaction
questions.correct_text: Requires the maximum leverage and its calculation methodology to be disclosed in the PPM
questions.explanation: Leverage is permitted subject to conditions, including disclosure of the maximum leverage and the methodology for calculating it in the placement memorandum. A PPM silent on the point cannot support the borrowing until it is amended.

questions.question: A VC scheme values its portfolio through the FME's own internal committee and computes NAV once a year. Which element is defective?
questions.option_A: Neither — annual NAV and internal valuation are both permitted for VC schemes
questions.option_B: The valuation, because it must be carried out by an independent service provider
questions.option_C: The NAV frequency, because venture capital schemes require quarterly computation
questions.option_D: Both, because VC schemes must value monthly and appoint an external administrator
questions.correct_text: The valuation, because it must be carried out by an independent service provider
questions.explanation: Annual NAV is permitted for a VC scheme provided the methodology is documented. Valuation, however, must be performed by an independent service provider — a fund administrator, custodian, registered CRA or IBBI-registered valuer. An internal committee does not satisfy that.

questions.question: An open-ended restricted scheme has raised USD 2.4 Million and wishes to take a 15% position in an unlisted company. The compliance officer should advise that:
questions.option_A: The investment is permitted, since 15% is comfortably within the 25% unlisted cap
questions.option_B: The investment is permitted only if the unlisted company is incorporated in the IFSC
questions.option_C: The investment must wait until the scheme achieves the USD 3 Million minimum corpus
questions.option_D: The scheme cannot invest in unlisted securities at all while it remains open-ended
questions.correct_text: The investment must wait until the scheme achieves the USD 3 Million minimum corpus
questions.explanation: The 25% cap is satisfied, but the second proviso to Reg. 35(1) inserted in 2026 bars unlisted investment altogether until the scheme achieves the USD 3 Million minimum corpus. Two separate conditions apply and both must be met.

questions.question: A restricted scheme proposes to buy an asset from an investor holding 55% of its commitments. Approval is obtained from 78% of investors by value, counting that investor's vote. The position is that:
questions.option_A: The approval is valid, since the 75% threshold by value has clearly been exceeded
questions.option_B: The approval is invalid, since such transactions require unanimous investor consent
questions.option_C: The approval is valid, provided the transaction is disclosed in the next annual report
questions.option_D: The approval is invalid, since the interested investor's votes must be excluded
questions.correct_text: The approval is invalid, since the interested investor's votes must be excluded
questions.explanation: Reg. 35(4) requires 75% approval by value excluding the votes of the investor concerned. Counting the 55% investor's own vote inflates the tally — the exclusion is precisely what makes the safeguard meaningful.

questions.question: A close-ended restricted scheme with a targeted corpus of USD 40 Million proposes an FME contribution of USD 900,000. The compliance officer should identify that this:
questions.option_A: Satisfies the floor, since USD 750,000 is the applicable minimum for close-ended schemes
questions.option_B: Falls short, because the floor for a corpus above USD 30 Million is USD 1,500,000
questions.option_C: Exceeds the ceiling, because contribution is capped at 2.5% of the targeted corpus
questions.option_D: Satisfies the floor, provided the balance is contributed before the scheme's first close
questions.correct_text: Satisfies the floor, since USD 750,000 is the applicable minimum for close-ended schemes
questions.explanation: For close-ended restricted schemes the floor is 2.5% of targeted corpus or USD 750,000, whichever is lower. The USD 1,500,000 figure belongs to the open-ended regime under Reg. 40(b). Confusing the two floors is the common error.

questions.question: A retail scheme's offer document is filed 24 working days before launch, with fiduciary approval scheduled for the following week. The compliance officer should identify that:
questions.option_A: Nothing is defective, since 24 working days exceeds the 21-working-day requirement
questions.option_B: The filing is premature, because fiduciary approval must precede the filing itself
questions.option_C: The filing is defective only if the Authority's comments are not incorporated in time
questions.option_D: The timeline should be 21 calendar days, so the filing is in fact earlier than required
questions.correct_text: The filing is premature, because fiduciary approval must precede the filing itself
questions.explanation: The 21-working-day timeline is met, but Reg. 43(5) bars filing a retail scheme at all until the fiduciaries have approved it. Sequence matters as much as timing — a compliant clock does not cure an out-of-order approval.

questions.question: Six months after closure a retail scheme has 26 investors, the largest holding 28% of the corpus. The correct assessment is that the scheme:
questions.option_A: Complies, because it exceeds the minimum of twenty investors within the cure period
questions.option_B: Complies, because the 25% ceiling applies only at the time the offer closes
questions.option_C: Breaches, because no single investor may exceed 25% once the cure period has expired
questions.option_D: Breaches, because a retail scheme requires at least fifty investors after six months
questions.correct_text: Breaches, because no single investor may exceed 25% once the cure period has expired
questions.explanation: Reg. 44 imposes two conditions to be achieved within six months of closure: at least twenty investors AND no single investor above 25%. The investor count is satisfied; the concentration limit is not.

questions.question: Investors holding 70% by value approve a two-year extension of a close-ended retail scheme's tenure. The FME proceeds on that basis. The defect is that:
questions.option_A: Two-thirds by value is insufficient; three-quarters approval is required for retail
questions.option_B: Extension of a close-ended retail scheme's tenure is not permitted in any circumstances
questions.option_C: The vote must be counted by number of investors rather than by value of holdings
questions.option_D: The approval of the Authority is also required, in addition to the investor vote
questions.correct_text: The approval of the Authority is also required, in addition to the investor vote
questions.explanation: Reg. 45(3) requires both two-thirds of investors by value AND the Authority's approval. The 70% vote satisfies the investor limb but not the regulatory one. Restricted schemes, by contrast, need only the investor resolution — a distinction worth holding.

questions.question: An SSF placement memorandum expired last week without the minimum corpus being achieved. The FME now applies to extend it. The compliance officer should advise that:
questions.option_A: The application is out of time, since extension must be sought while the PPM is valid
questions.option_B: The extension is available on payment of 50% of the fresh-scheme filing fee
questions.option_C: Multiple extensions are available at 25% and then 50% of the fresh-scheme fee
questions.option_D: The extension is automatic, the memorandum reviving on payment of the prescribed fee
questions.correct_text: The application is out of time, since extension must be sought while the PPM is valid
questions.explanation: The one-time six-month extension at 50% of the fresh-scheme fee exists, but it must be sought while the memorandum is still valid. Once it has lapsed there is nothing to extend. Note also that the multi-extension regime added in 2026 applies to restricted schemes, not SSFs.

questions.question: An Authorised FME proposes an open-ended special situation fund that will act as a resolution applicant under the IBC. The compliance officer should identify:
questions.option_A: One defect — only the open-ended structure, since any FME may launch an SSF
questions.option_B: Two defects — the FME category and the open-ended structure are both impermissible
questions.option_C: One defect — only the FME category, since an SSF may be open- or close-ended
questions.option_D: No defect — acting as a resolution applicant is expressly permitted for an SSF
questions.correct_text: Two defects — the FME category and the open-ended structure are both impermissible
questions.explanation: Acting as a resolution applicant is permitted (Reg. 54(2)), but an SSF may be launched only by a Registered FME and must be close-ended (Reg. 56(1)). Two independent defects — the permitted activity is a distraction from both.

questions.question: A Registered FME (Non-Retail) proposes an unlisted ETF marketed only to accredited investors. The compliance officer should identify that:
questions.option_A: Only the listing is defective, since any Registered FME may launch an ETF
questions.option_B: Only the category is defective, since accredited-investor ETFs need not be listed
questions.option_C: Both the category and the listing are defective, whatever the investor profile
questions.option_D: Neither is defective, provided the offer document discloses the absence of listing
questions.correct_text: Both the category and the listing are defective, whatever the investor profile
questions.explanation: Reg. 61(1) confines ETFs to a Registered FME (Retail), and Reg. 61(5) makes listing mandatory. Restricting the offer to accredited investors does not relax either requirement — investor sophistication is not a substitute for category or listing.

questions.question: A Gold ETF holds 88% of AUM in physical gold and 9% in gold ETCDs, intending to take physical delivery. The correct assessment is that:
questions.option_A: Both limbs are satisfied, since ETCD exposure remains below the 10% ceiling
questions.option_B: The ETCD position breaches the ceiling once the delivery intention is disclosed
questions.option_C: Neither limb applies, because physical-delivery Gold ETFs are exempt from both
questions.option_D: The 90% floor is breached, though the ETCD position is within its own limit
questions.correct_text: The 90% floor is breached, though the ETCD position is within its own limit
questions.explanation: Reg. 65(1) requires at least 90% of AUM in gold and gold-related instruments; 88% falls short. The ETCD limb is satisfied, and the physical-delivery proviso relaxes the ETCD cap rather than the 90% floor.

questions.question: An Investment Trust raises funds privately from 45 investors, of whom 40 invest USD 300,000 each and 5 are accredited investors investing USD 100,000 each. The position is that:
questions.option_A: The placement is compliant on both the investor count and the investment thresholds
questions.option_B: The placement is defective, because every investor must invest at least USD 250,000
questions.option_C: The placement is defective, because accredited investors cannot be counted separately
questions.option_D: The placement is compliant only if the five accredited investors are institutions
questions.correct_text: The placement is compliant on both the investor count and the investment thresholds
questions.explanation: Reg. 93 permits investors investing at least USD 250,000 OR accredited investors, capped at fifty. Forty-five investors, with the smaller tickets coming from accredited investors, satisfies both limbs — the two categories are alternatives, not cumulative conditions.

questions.question: For a public issue, an investment manager files the draft offer document 30 working days before the exchange filing, and the final offer document 3 working days before the offer opens. The defect is:
questions.option_A: The draft filing, which must precede the exchange filing by 21 working days
questions.option_B: The final filing, which must be made not less than five working days before opening
questions.option_C: Both filings, since the draft requires 45 working days and the final requires ten
questions.option_D: Neither — both timelines comply with the requirements for a public issue
questions.correct_text: The final filing, which must be made not less than five working days before opening
questions.explanation: The draft timeline of not less than thirty working days is met. The final offer document, however, must be filed not less than five working days before the offer opens (Reg. 94(g)); three is short.

questions.question: A fund of funds scheme with AUM of USD 120 Million invests in underlying schemes that have each appointed independent custodians. The compliance officer should conclude that the FoF:
questions.option_A: Must appoint its own custodian, since its AUM exceeds the USD 70 Million threshold
questions.option_B: Must appoint a custodian based in the IFSC within twenty-four months of the amendment
questions.option_C: Need not appoint a custodian, because the underlying schemes have independent custodians
questions.option_D: Need not appoint a custodian only if all of its investors are accredited investors
questions.correct_text: Need not appoint a custodian, because the underlying schemes have independent custodians
questions.explanation: The AUM threshold in Reg. 132 would ordinarily bite, but the proviso exempts a fund of funds where the underlying scheme(s) have appointed independent custodians. The exemption turns on the underlying arrangement, not on size or investor type.

questions.question: An FME files the scheme annual report with the Authority five months after financial year end, and supplies the full report to a requesting investor 20 days after the request. The defects are:
questions.option_A: Only the filing, since there is no prescribed period for responding to investors
questions.option_B: Only the investor response, since six months is allowed for the Authority filing
questions.option_C: Neither — both fall within the periods the regulation currently prescribes
questions.option_D: Both — the report is one month late and the investor response exceeds fifteen days
questions.correct_text: Both — the report is one month late and the investor response exceeds fifteen days
questions.explanation: Reg. 134(1) requires filing within four months, so five months is late. The full report must reach a requesting investor within fifteen days. Note the six-month extension was approved in July 2026 but is not yet notified — the four-month clock still binds.

questions.question: A director resigns from an FME after a scheme mis-selling issue arises, relying on an indemnity in her appointment letter. The correct position is that she:
questions.option_A: Remains liable for acts of commission or omission notwithstanding the indemnity
questions.option_B: Is released from liability once the resignation takes effect and notice is served
questions.option_C: Remains liable only for the period during which she actually held office
questions.option_D: Is released, provided the investors were informed of the indemnity arrangement
questions.correct_text: Remains liable for acts of commission or omission notwithstanding the indemnity
questions.explanation: The Code of Conduct provides that the FME, its directors, partners and officers are not absolved of liability to the scheme or investors for acts of commission or omission, notwithstanding any contract, agreement or termination. Resignation and indemnity change nothing.

questions.question: An FME aggregates its scheme expenses at entity level and allocates them across schemes annually on a reasonable basis, disclosing a single overall expense cap in each PPM. The defect is that expenses must be:
questions.option_A: Capped at 2% of assets under management for every scheme by the regulations
questions.option_B: Identified and appropriated separately per scheme, with each item a distinct line
questions.option_C: Disclosed to the fiduciaries of each scheme rather than to the scheme's investors
questions.option_D: Allocated quarterly rather than annually, though entity-level pooling is permitted
questions.correct_text: Identified and appropriated separately per scheme, with each item a distinct line
questions.explanation: Reg. 128 requires fees and expenses to be clearly identified and appropriated separately for each scheme, with maximum fees and each expense item disclosed as a specific line item. Pooling and a single aggregate cap defeats both requirements.

questions.question: Investors holding 62% by value resolve to wind up a scheme; the FME declines to act, arguing the threshold is unmet. The compliance officer should confirm that:
questions.option_A: The FME is incorrect, because a simple majority by value suffices for winding up
questions.option_B: The FME is correct, but only because the resolution was not passed at a meeting
questions.option_C: The FME is correct, because seventy-five per cent by value is required to wind up
questions.option_D: The FME is incorrect, because the threshold is two-thirds of investors by value
questions.correct_text: The FME is correct, because seventy-five per cent by value is required to wind up
questions.explanation: Reg. 131(1)(b) requires seventy-five per cent of investors by value, at a meeting of investors. At 62% the resolution falls short. Two-thirds is the retail tenure-extension threshold — a different provision entirely.

questions.question: During an inspection the FME directs that only its Principal Officer and Compliance Officer will engage with the inspecting authority. The defect is that the duty to assist binds:
questions.option_A: Only those officers specifically named in the inspection order made by the Authority
questions.option_B: The board of directors collectively, rather than officers acting in their own right
questions.option_C: Only the Principal Officer, the Compliance Officer and the appointed statutory auditor
questions.option_D: Every officer, partner, trustee, director, CEO, KMP, employee and agent of the FME
questions.correct_text: Every officer, partner, trustee, director, CEO, KMP, employee and agent of the FME
questions.explanation: Reg. 139 casts the duty to assist and furnish records on the FME and a wide list of persons connected with it. Channelling an inspection through two officers is itself a failure to co-operate, independent of whatever the inspection finds.

questions.question: A restricted scheme obtained one six-month PPM extension in March and now seeks a second. Post the January 2026 Amendment, the fee for this second extension is:
questions.option_A: 50% of the fee for filing a fresh scheme, as prevalent at the time of the extension
questions.option_B: 25% of the fee for filing a fresh scheme, as the same rate applies to each extension
questions.option_C: 100% of the fresh-scheme filing fee, since only one extension attracts a concession
questions.option_D: Nil, because the fee is payable only on the first extension of the memorandum
questions.correct_text: 50% of the fee for filing a fresh scheme, as prevalent at the time of the extension
questions.explanation: The 2026 regime allows multiple extensions at 25% for the first and 50% thereafter, computed on the fee for filing a fresh scheme as prevalent at the time of extension — not the fee originally paid.

questions.question: An FME provides third-party fund management services under an arrangement in which the foreign manager fully indemnifies it against investor claims. The FME's liability:
questions.option_A: Transfers to the third-party manager to the extent of the indemnity provided
questions.option_B: Continues in full, notwithstanding any indemnification arrangement between them
questions.option_C: Is shared between them in the proportions set out in the governing arrangement
questions.option_D: Ceases upon the Authority granting authorisation for the arrangement in writing
questions.correct_text: Continues in full, notwithstanding any indemnification arrangement between them
questions.explanation: Reg. 107C(4) preserves the FME's liability in full despite any indemnity. An indemnity may allocate loss between the parties commercially, but it cannot displace the FME's regulatory responsibility to investors.

questions.question: A close-ended restricted scheme resolves, by 80% of investors by value, to move NAV computation from semi-annual to annual, citing the July 2026 approval. The compliance officer should advise that:
questions.option_A: The change is effective, since the investor threshold of 75% by value is exceeded
questions.option_B: The change requires the Authority's prior approval in addition to the investor vote
questions.option_C: The change cannot take effect yet, because the amendment has not been notified
questions.option_D: The change is effective only for schemes whose corpus exceeds USD 3 Million
questions.correct_text: The change cannot take effect yet, because the amendment has not been notified
questions.explanation: Even though the 75%-by-value condition attaching to the approved change is satisfied, the amendment has not been notified. Until it is, the existing NAV requirement governs. Approval sets direction; notification creates the obligation.

questions.question: Authorised FME minimum net worth: USD ___
questions.explanation: Second Schedule — Authorised FME.

questions.question: Registered FME (Non-Retail) minimum net worth: USD ___
questions.explanation: Second Schedule — Registered FME (Non-Retail).

questions.question: Registered FME (Retail) minimum net worth: USD ___
questions.explanation: Second Schedule — Registered FME (Retail).

questions.question: Net worth must be met on the date of application and re-tested only annually.
questions.explanation: Reg. 8(1): the net worth requirement shall be maintained at ALL times.

questions.question: A branch FME may maintain the minimum net worth at parent level, earmarked for the IFSC branch.
questions.explanation: Reg. 8(2) and its proviso — maintained at parent level, but earmarked for the branch.

questions.question: Which is NOT correct about the FME net worth requirement?
questions.option_A: It is calculated separately for each scheme launched
questions.option_B: It must be maintained at all times
questions.option_C: A branch may hold it at parent level if earmarked
questions.option_D: It is separate from, and additional to, other activity requirements
questions.correct_text: It is calculated separately for each scheme launched
questions.explanation: Net worth attaches to the FME by category — it is not computed per scheme. The other three are correct (Reg. 8(1),(2),(3)).

questions.question: Match each FME category to its minimum net worth.
questions.explanation: Second Schedule.
questions.pairs: Authorised FME = USD 75,000 ; Registered FME (Non-Retail) = USD 500,000 ; Registered FME (Retail) = USD 1,000,000

questions.question: Base KMP experience requirement: at least ___ years in related activities.
questions.explanation: Reg. 7(5)(b) as substituted w.e.f. 30.01.2026.

questions.question: A KMP with a professional qualification needs only 3 years' experience for the role under sub-regulation (2).
questions.explanation: First proviso to Reg. 7(5)(b) — three years where the KMP holds a professional qualification.

questions.question: A venture capital scheme may have at most ___ investors.
questions.explanation: Chapter III Part A — VC scheme investor cap.

questions.question: Minimum investment by an investor in a VC scheme: USD ___
questions.explanation: VC scheme minimum ticket (employees/directors: USD 60,000).

questions.question: A VC scheme must deploy at least ___% of investible funds within the stated period.
questions.explanation: The 80% / 10-year deployment rule for VC schemes.

questions.question: The minimum corpus of a VC scheme is USD 5 Million.
questions.explanation: The minimum corpus is USD 3 Million (with a USD 200 Million ceiling).

questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes a VC scheme from a Restricted scheme on investor limits?
questions.option_A: Both allow up to 1,000 investors
questions.option_B: VC is capped at 50 investors (USD 250,000 ticket); Restricted allows up to 1,000 (USD 150,000 ticket)
questions.option_C: VC allows 1,000 and Restricted 50
questions.option_D: Neither has an investor cap
questions.correct_text: VC is capped at 50 investors (USD 250,000 ticket); Restricted allows up to 1,000 (USD 150,000 ticket)
questions.explanation: VC schemes are capped at 50 investors with a USD 250,000 ticket; Restricted schemes allow up to 1,000 investors at USD 150,000.

questions.question: Restricted schemes may have at most ___ investors.
Minimum investment in a restricted scheme: USD ___
questions.explanation: Reg. 32(2) — employees/directors of the FME: USD 40,000.

questions.question: Employees or directors of the FME may invest in a restricted scheme from USD ___
questions.explanation: Proviso to Reg. 32(2).

questions.question: Minimum corpus of a restricted scheme: USD ___ Million
An open-ended restricted scheme may commence investment activity on raising USD 1 Million.
questions.explanation: Proviso to Reg. 35(2) — and it must reach the USD 3 Million minimum corpus within 12 months.

questions.question: An open-ended restricted scheme may invest in unlisted securities before reaching USD 3 Million corpus.
questions.explanation: Second proviso to Reg. 35(1), inserted w.e.f. 30.01.2026: unlisted investment only upon achieving the USD 3 Million minimum corpus.

questions.question: Open-ended structure is available to restricted schemes filed as:
questions.option_A: Category I only
questions.option_B: Category II only
questions.option_C: Category III only
questions.option_D: All three categories
questions.correct_text: Category III only
questions.explanation: Reg. 30(2): schemes under clauses (a) and (c) — Category I and II — are filed close-ended; only clause (b) (Category III) may be open- or close-ended.

questions.question: Maximum investment in unlisted securities by an open-ended restricted scheme: ___% of corpus
A retail scheme's draft offer document must be filed at least ___ working days before launch.
A retail scheme must have at least ___ investors.
questions.explanation: Reg. 44 — with no single investor above 25%, achieved within 6 months of closure.

questions.question: No single investor may hold more than ___% of a retail scheme.
questions.explanation: Reg. 44.

questions.question: A retail scheme may be constituted in IFSC as a company, LLP or trust.
questions.explanation: Reg. 45(4): retail schemes shall be constituted as a Company or Trust only. LLP is available to restricted schemes (Reg. 33(5)).

questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes retail from restricted close-ended tenure extension?
questions.option_A: Both need only investor approval
questions.option_B: Retail needs only the Authority; restricted needs only investors
questions.option_C: Neither may be extended
questions.option_D: Retail needs 2/3 of investors AND the Authority; restricted needs only 2/3 of investors
questions.correct_text: Retail needs 2/3 of investors AND the Authority; restricted needs only 2/3 of investors
questions.explanation: Reg. 45(3) requires two-thirds of investors by value AND the Authority's approval for retail. Reg. 33(3) requires only two-thirds for restricted.

questions.question: A retail scheme may be filed with the Authority before the fiduciaries have approved it.
questions.explanation: Reg. 43(5): no retail scheme shall be filed unless it has been approved by the fiduciaries.

questions.question: A special situation fund may be launched as an open-ended scheme.
questions.explanation: Reg. 56(1): a special situation fund shall ONLY be a close-ended fund.

questions.question: Minimum tenure of a special situation fund: ___ years
Which is correct about extending an SSF placement memorandum's validity?
questions.option_A: A one-time six-month extension on payment of 50% of the fresh-scheme fee
questions.option_B: Unlimited extensions at 25% then 50% of the fee
questions.option_C: A one-time twelve-month extension, free of charge
questions.option_D: No extension is available
questions.correct_text: A one-time six-month extension on payment of 50% of the fresh-scheme fee
questions.explanation: Reg. 55(3): a ONE-TIME option to extend by six months on paying 50% of a fresh-scheme fee. The multi-extension regime added in 2026 applies to restricted schemes, not SSFs.

questions.question: Any Registered FME may launch an Exchange Traded Fund.
questions.explanation: Reg. 61(1): only Registered FMEs (Retail) may launch ETFs.

questions.question: A Gold ETF must invest at least ___% of AUM in gold or bullion instruments.
Exposure to gold ETCDs must not exceed ___% of a Gold ETF's AUM.
questions.explanation: Proviso to Reg. 65(1) — not applicable where the intention is to take physical delivery.

questions.question: ETF units must be mandatorily listed and traded on a recognised stock exchange.
questions.explanation: Reg. 61(5), reinforced by Reg. 110.

questions.question: Which scheme does NOT mandatorily require an independent custodian?
questions.option_A: A retail scheme
questions.option_B: A fund of funds whose underlying schemes already have independent custodians
questions.option_C: An open-ended restricted scheme
questions.option_D: A scheme managing AUM of USD 90 Million
questions.correct_text: A fund of funds whose underlying schemes already have independent custodians
questions.explanation: Reg. 132 lists retail schemes, open-ended restricted schemes and all other schemes above USD 70 Million AUM. A fund of funds is exempt where the underlying scheme(s) have appointed independent custodians.

questions.question: Custodian appointment threshold for other schemes: AUM above USD ___ Million
The scheme annual report must reach the Authority within ___ months of financial year end.
questions.explanation: Reg. 134(1). The extension to six months was approved on 24.07.2026 but is NOT yet notified.

questions.question: A scheme's auditor may be a firm associated with the FME if the fiduciaries approve.
questions.explanation: Reg. 135(1): the auditor must not be in any way associated with the FME. The fiduciaries appoint (135(2)) but cannot cure association.

questions.question: On an investor's request, the full annual report must be provided within ___ days.
questions.explanation: Proviso to Reg. 134(3).

questions.question: Investors must be given information about their holdings at the end of every month.
questions.explanation: Reg. 136(1) — and within ten working days of a request.

questions.question: A scheme may be wound up if ___% of investors by value so resolve.
The 2026 Amendment inserted which pair of new winding-up grounds?
questions.option_A: A 50% investor resolution and a NAV trigger
questions.option_B: Authority suo motu determination and auditor resignation
questions.option_C: A failed raise where validity was not extended; and a scheme with no investors and no funds collected
questions.option_D: Custodian resignation and two qualified reports
questions.correct_text: A failed raise where validity was not extended; and a scheme with no investors and no funds collected
questions.explanation: Reg. 131(1)(c) — funds raised, minimum corpus missed within (extended) validity and the FME has NOT filed and paid for a further extension; and Reg. 131(1)(d) — no investors onboarded, no funds collected, and the FME voluntarily winds up.

questions.question: The 25% FME contribution ceiling approved on 24 July 2026 binds FMEs today.
questions.explanation: Approval is not notification. Reg. 28(1)'s 10% ceiling still binds until the amendment is notified.

questions.question: Under the approved blended-finance framework, minimum investment in junior unit classes will be:
questions.option_A: USD 250,000 for all investors
questions.option_C: No minimum
questions.option_D: USD 1 Million (non-individual Accredited Investors) or USD 2 Million (others)
questions.correct_text: USD 1 Million (non-individual Accredited Investors) or USD 2 Million (others)
questions.explanation: USD 1 Million from non-individual Accredited Investors, or USD 2 Million from other investors.

lessons.title: Learn the concepts
lessons.hook: Day one at GreenGate Ventures. Your first call: register with the cheapest category (USD 75K net worth) and upgrade later when the retail dream arrives?
lessons.cards: Three doors into GIFT City fund management: LAW The framework recognises Authorised FMEs, Registered FMEs (Non-Retail) and Registered FMEs (Retail). | PLAIN An ascending ladder of trust. Authorised: VC schemes and single-family funds. Non-Retail adds restricted schemes, PMS and private REIT/InvIT management. Retail sits on top: retail schemes, ETFs, public REIT/InvIT offers — plus everything below. | WATCH Each tier inherits ALL activities of the tiers beneath it. A Retail FME never needs a second registration to run a VC scheme. || The net worth ladder: LAW Minimum net worth: USD 75,000 (Authorised), USD 500,000 (Non-Retail), USD 1,000,000 (Retail) — at all times. | PLAIN The price of each door. And it is a continuous obligation — dipping below the line mid-year is a breach even if you were compliant at registration. | WATCH Branches hold net worth at the PARENT level — but the parent must ensure the branch has operating funds. And FME net worth is separate from and additional to net worth needed for any other regulated activity. || Getting in, switching, getting out: LAW Deficient applications get 30 days to cure. Category change needs prior Authority approval. Surrender is effective only on acceptance. | PLAIN IFSCA controls all three gates. You cannot drift between categories by conduct, and you remain a regulated (and liable) entity until the Authority formally accepts your exit. | WATCH Meeting the higher net worth does NOT auto-upgrade you — Reg. 13(2) requires prior approval for any category change. || Stay in your lane: LAW An FME shall not undertake business activities other than those specified, without prior approval of the Authority. | PLAIN The activity perimeter is closed by default. Even a branch acting on its home regulator’s approval for an outside-IFSC activity must inform IFSCA within 15 days. | WATCH Opening a marketing or client-service office in another jurisdiction needs PRIOR intimation — not post-facto.
lessons.tip: Regulators read your net worth position before anything else. Maintain a quarterly net worth working paper signed off by the Principal Officer — a deficiency you self-report with a remediation plan is a conversation; one IFSCA discovers first is a warning letter.

lessons.title: Learn the concepts
lessons.hook: Your Principal Officer suggests the Compliance Officer should report to her — "cleaner lines, faster decisions." Do you sign off on that org chart?
lessons.cards: Two people every FME must have: LAW Every FME appoints a Principal Officer — responsible overall for fund management, risk management and compliance — and an additional KMP designated as Compliance Officer. | PLAIN The PO is the apex accountable human; the CO is the professional conscience. Between them, everything the FME does has a name attached to it. | WATCH The 2022 regulations called the second KMP the "Compliance and Risk Manager". The 2025 text renamed it Compliance Officer. Old study material will betray you here. || The CO reports past the PO: LAW The Compliance Officer is a senior officer reporting to the board of directors — or the head of the organisation where there is no board. | PLAIN Independence is hard-wired: the person monitoring compliance does not report to the person running the funds. The CO must also be capable of understanding financial statements and the regulatory requirements. | WATCH 2022 said "financially literate and capable of appreciating"; 2025 sharpened it to "capable of understanding the financial statements". Small words, favourite trap. || When two KMPs become three: LAW A Retail FME appoints an additional fund-management KMP BEFORE filing the offer document of its first retail scheme or ETF. Any FME crossing USD 1 billion AUM at FY-close (excluding FoF AUM) does the same. | PLAIN Scale and public money both demand a dedicated fund-management brain, separate from the PO. | WATCH The USD 1bn test EXCLUDES fund of funds AUM — those assets are managed at the underlying level. And the retail trigger is pre-FILING, not pre-launch. || Fit and proper — always, everyone: LAW The applicant, PO, directors/partners, KMPs and controlling shareholders must be fit and proper at all times: financial integrity, good reputation and character, honesty. | PLAIN Three positive limbs, applied continuously, to everyone who matters. A conviction involving moral turpitude or an economic offence breaks it. | WATCH The January 2026 Amendment rebuilt the KMP experience routes: 5 years base, 3 years with a professional qualification, and 2/3-year certification paths. If you learned the old Reg. 7 experience rules, relearn them.
lessons.tip: Build a hiring pack for every KMP: experience certificates, qualification proofs, fit-and-proper declarations and the appointing resolution, filed together. Reviews ask for the appointment chain — an org chart alone answers nothing.

lessons.title: Learn the concepts
lessons.hook: The founders ask: "Can we launch Climate Fund I without putting in a single dollar of our own?"
lessons.cards: Who gets in — and how many: LAW A VC scheme shall not have more than fifty (50) investors; non-accredited investors invest at least USD 250,000; FME employees/directors at USD 60,000. | PLAIN An exclusive room: 50 sophisticated cheques maximum. The 250K ticket is the sophistication filter; accredited investors skip it. | WATCH "At least" 250K — exactly 250K qualifies (2022 said "above"). And 2022 capped at 49 investors ("less than fifty"). Both flipped in 2025. Joint investors combining to 250K: only spouse, parent, or child. || The size of the pool: LAW Minimum corpus USD 3 Million; total corpus shall not exceed USD 200 Million. | PLAIN Both a floor and a ceiling — VC is the only mainstream scheme with a cap. Bigger ambitions route through restricted schemes. | WATCH Restricted schemes share the 3M floor but have NO ceiling. Don’t transplant the 200M cap. || The 80/10 rule — keeping venture "venture": LAW At least 80% of corpus goes to investee companies within 10 years of incorporation (or schemes meeting that test). | PLAIN Four-fifths of the money must reach genuinely young companies. This is what stops a VC label on a late-stage PE fund. | WATCH Ten years from INCORPORATION of the investee — not from its funding round, not from scheme launch. || Skin in the game: LAW FME/associate invests ≥2.5% of targeted corpus (≤USD 30M schemes) or ≥USD 750,000 (>USD 30M), never exceeding 10%. | PLAIN The manager eats its own cooking. The floor aligns incentives; the 10% ceiling stops the FME dominating its own fund. | WATCH USD 750,000 is just 2.5% of 30M, frozen. And relocated schemes (moving to IFSC from abroad) are exempt entirely. || Conflicts and rhythm: LAW Associate investments need prior approval of 75% of investors by value. NAV at least annually, documented methodology; valuation by independents; leverage as disclosed in the PPM. | PLAIN Conflicted deals are democratised, not banned. And the compliance rhythm is annual — venture portfolios don’t need daily NAVs, they need methodological discipline. | WATCH 75% by VALUE, PRIOR — ratification after the cheque doesn’t cure it. And "VC schemes can’t borrow" is a myth: leverage is a disclosure matter.
lessons.tip: Keep the sponsor-commitment evidence as one file: board resolution approving the contribution, subscription agreement, and proof of capital. When a scheme is examined, commitment evidence is typically the first thing asked for — assembling it under deadline is how clean funds produce messy findings.

lessons.title: Learn the concepts
lessons.hook: Horizon Fund has raised USD 1.4M. The desk finds a hot pre-IPO deal — well within the 25% unlisted cap. They need your sign-off by noon.
lessons.cards: The bigger tent: LAW Restricted schemes may have up to 1,000 investors. Schemes filed as Category I and II AIFs must be close-ended; Category III may be open- or close-ended. | PLAIN Twenty times the VC room, same sophistication filter (private placement to accredited/threshold investors). Structure follows strategy: locked capital for illiquid Cat I/II plays; open-ended only for Cat III. | WATCH The 50-investor cap is VC-only. Retail schemes have no cap at all. Keep the three numbers separate: 50 / 1,000 / unlimited. || Start small, prove yourself: LAW An open-ended restricted scheme may commence investing at USD 1 Million, achieving the USD 3 Million minimum corpus within 12 months. | PLAIN A two-step launch ladder: start at 1M, prove you can reach 3M within a year of the taken-on-record communication. | WATCH Post the January 2026 Amendment, unlisted securities are OFF-LIMITS until the 3M is actually achieved — commencing at 1M does not open the unlisted door. || The 25% unlisted cap: LAW Open-ended restricted schemes cap unlisted securities at 25% of corpus — with a look-through exception for FoFs whose underlying open-ended schemes each respect the cap. | PLAIN Redemption liquidity and illiquid paper don’t mix, so open-ended structures get a hard limit. Close-ended schemes face no such cap. | WATCH The post-2026 test is TWO-step: (1) corpus ≥ 3M? If no — zero unlisted. (2) If yes — stay within 25%. Checking only the cap is the pre-amendment reflex. || Doubled skin for open doors: LAW Close-ended: ≥2.5% or ≥USD 750K (>30M). Open-ended: ≥5% or ≥USD 1.5M (>30M). Both capped at 10%. | PLAIN When investors can redeem, manager-investor misalignment bites harder — so open-ended floors are exactly double the close-ended ones. | WATCH Same 750K logic as VC, but the open-ended big-scheme floor is 1.5M. Four numbers, one pattern: close 2.5%/750K, open 5%/1.5M. || Conflicted trades and co-investments: LAW Buying/selling from associates, other schemes, or a 50%+ committed investor needs 75%-by-value approval — EXCLUDING the conflicted investor’s votes. Co-investment via segregated portfolios must never be on more favourable terms than the common portfolio; SPV leverage as disclosed. | PLAIN The supermajority returns, now with a twist: the mega-investor whose trade it is doesn’t get to vote on it. And co-investors may get access, never advantage. | WATCH "Not more favourable" — identical terms are fine, better terms are the breach.
lessons.tip: For open-ended schemes, run a two-line pre-trade check on every unlisted deal: (1) corpus ≥ USD 3M? (2) unlisted ≤ 25% post-trade? Have the fund accountant confirm both in writing — the email trail is your defence file.

lessons.title: Learn the concepts
lessons.hook: Marketing wants the retail scheme live in three weeks — "the offer document is basically final." Can you promise them a launch date?
lessons.cards: Public money, prior review: LAW No retail scheme launches unless the draft offer document was filed with IFSCA at least 21 working days before launch, with fees; Authority comments must be incorporated BEFORE launch. | PLAIN Private placements get a green channel; public money gets a runway. The regulator reads before the public buys. | WATCH WORKING days, not calendar days — 19 working days is a breach, not a rounding error. Validity: 12 months from taken-on-record. || The 20/25 rule: LAW At least 20 investors; no single investor above 25% — achieved within 6 months of closure of the offer. | PLAIN Genuine pooling, not one whale wearing a retail costume. The 6-month cure window makes the rule practical: a 30% investor at closing is curable, not fatal. | WATCH Contrast the logic: VC/restricted CAP investors (exclusivity); retail sets a FLOOR (genuine distribution). || Form and fiduciaries: LAW Retail schemes: company or trust ONLY. Fiduciaries must approve the scheme BEFORE filing; appointing a retail fiduciary itself needs prior Authority approval. | PLAIN Two locks before the regulator even sees the document: an Authority-approved fiduciary, and that fiduciary’s sign-off on the scheme. | WATCH No LLP option for retail schemes — the one legal form the framework withholds. "Circulated to trustees for information" is not approval. || Time and the exit door: LAW Close-ended retail schemes: minimum 3-year tenure; extension up to 2 years needs two-thirds of investors by value AND Authority approval. | PLAIN For sophisticated schemes, investor supermajority alone extends tenure. Retail adds the regulator as a second lock. | WATCH The extra Authority layer is the retail signature — spot it and you can reverse-engineer which scheme type a question is about.
lessons.tip: The moment you file a retail offer document, diary two dates: the 21-working-day launch gate and the 12-month validity expiry. Most retail timing breaches are calendar failures, not judgment failures — the diary IS the compliance control.

lessons.title: Learn the concepts
lessons.hook: A renewables company enters CIRP. The investment team asks: "Can our fund actually walk into an NCLT process and bid for the company itself?"
lessons.cards: The distressed-asset specialist: LAW A special situation fund invests in special situation assets and may act as a resolution applicant under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016. | PLAIN The bridge between IFSC capital and Indian insolvency resolution — an SSF can walk into a CIRP and bid for the company itself. | WATCH Launched by a REGISTERED FME via private placement. Authorised FMEs (VC + family funds only) cannot. || Locked capital, long game: LAW SSFs are close-ended only, minimum tenure 3 years; extension up to 2 years with two-thirds by value; beyond that, only willing investors stay and dissenters get an exit. | PLAIN Distressed strategies and redemption liquidity are structurally incompatible. The extension ladder ends in pure consent: past year five, nobody is locked in against their will. | WATCH Beyond the 2-year extension it is NOT another vote — it’s express consent of the willing plus an exit for the rest. || The extension asymmetry — 2026’s sharpest trap: LAW If an SSF misses its minimum corpus, it has a ONE-TIME option to extend the PPM by 6 months at 50% of the fresh-scheme fee. | PLAIN This is the pre-2026 rule — and for SSFs it still IS the rule. The January 2026 Amendment moved VC and restricted schemes to multiple extensions (25% first, 50% after, filed while the PPM is valid) but left Reg. 55(3) untouched. | WATCH One framework, two extension regimes. If a question doesn’t specify the scheme type, the extension answer is "it depends" — and that’s the point.
lessons.tip: At SSF launch, write the corpus-timeline memo: PPM validity, the SINGLE 6-month extension, the 50% fee. Boards assume the multi-extension regime applies to everything post-2026 — pre-empt that assumption in writing before the fundraise runs slow.

lessons.title: Learn the concepts
lessons.hook: The product team wants your Gold ETF to hold 30% in gold derivatives — "same exposure, better liquidity." Approve?
lessons.cards: The retail-only, exchange-anchored product: LAW Only Registered FMEs (Retail) may launch ETFs — draft offer document 21 working days before launch, 12-month validity, and MANDATORY listing on a recognised stock exchange. | PLAIN An ETF is retail DNA plus market plumbing: the retail filing discipline applies, and an unlisted ETF is a contradiction the framework doesn’t permit. | WATCH The permitted menu: Equity Index, Debt Index, Commodity, Hybrid (2+ asset classes), Actively Managed, and others with exchange + Authority approval. Yes — ACTIVELY managed ETFs are expressly allowed. || The 90/10 metal tests: LAW Gold and Silver ETFs: at least 90% of AUM in the metal or bullion instruments (including BDRs); exposure to ETCDs with that metal underlying capped at 10%. | PLAIN Purity tests — an investor buying a Gold ETF gets gold, not a derivatives book wearing a gold label. | WATCH Physical gold sits in a vault REGISTERED WITH THE AUTHORITY, physically verified by an independent agency HALF-YEARLY, reported within 2 months of each half-year end. || Fund of funds — the look-through machine: LAW A FoF invests in other schemes (IFSC, India or foreign), except funds needed for expenses, hedging, or redemption/distribution liquidity as disclosed. | PLAIN A FoF holds schemes, not securities — the carve-outs are narrow and disclosure-bound. And the framework consistently refuses to duplicate protections that exist at the underlying level. | WATCH Three look-throughs to remember: FoF valuation exemption (underlying independently valued), FoF custody exemption (underlying has custodians), FoF exclusion from the USD 1bn KMP test.
lessons.tip: Calendar the vault verification cycle at launch: independent physical verification every half-year, reported within 2 months of the half-year end. A missing verification report is the easiest ETF finding an examiner can write — and the cheapest one to prevent.

lessons.title: Learn the concepts
lessons.hook: The InvIT client wants the public offer open within a fortnight of receiving IFSCA observations. Do you commit to that timeline?
lessons.cards: Two lanes for Investment Trusts: LAW Private placement: at least USD 250,000 per investor or accredited investors, maximum 50 — final placement memorandum filed within 10 working days of allotment. Public offers run the full review cycle. | PLAIN REITs and InvITs mirror the scheme logic: a fast sophisticated lane with post-facto filing, and a slow public lane with pre-facto everything. | WATCH The private lane’s thresholds are the VC scheme’s thresholds — 250K and 50. The framework reuses its own furniture. || The public lane, step by step: LAW Draft offer document ≥30 working days before the formal filing; public comments ≥14 days on four websites; due diligence certificate by the IM or investment banker; Authority observations within 30 working days of filing or 21 from a satisfactory reply — whichever is LATER. | PLAIN A public offer is a sequence of checkpoints, each with an owner and a clock. The "whichever is later" formula means sloppy query responses restart the regulator’s clock, never shorten it. | WATCH The comment window is 14 DAYS; the draft filing runway is 30 WORKING days. Mixing the units is the classic error. || Last gates and shelf life: LAW Final offer document filed with exchange(s) and Authority ≥5 working days before opening. The offer must be made within 1 year of observations — else file a fresh draft. | PLAIN A five-day final buffer, and a 12-month expiry on the regulator’s green light. Market disclosures go stale; the framework refuses to let last year’s review bless this year’s offer. | WATCH Miss the 1-year window and there’s no confirmatory-letter shortcut — the entire draft-and-observation cycle restarts.
lessons.tip: Answer IFSCA queries completely in ONE round. The observation clock is "30 working days from filing or 21 from a satisfactory reply — whichever is LATER": a partial reply doesn’t save time, it restarts the regulator’s clock and costs you weeks.

lessons.title: Learn the concepts
lessons.hook: The CFO says: "Climate Fund I is close-ended — so no custodian needed, right?"
lessons.cards: Who must have a custodian: LAW Independent custodian mandatory for: retail schemes; open-ended restricted schemes; and any scheme with AUM above USD 70 Million. FoF exemption where underlying schemes have custodians. | PLAIN Three triggers — public money, redemption pressure, and sheer size. Miss all three and custody is your choice, not your obligation. | WATCH The USD 70M trigger catches CLOSE-ended restricted schemes too, once they grow. "We’re close-ended so no custodian" is only half a rule. || Where the custodian sits — and the 24-month runway: LAW The custodian must be IFSC-based, except where local laws of the issuing jurisdiction mandate local custody. The 2026 Amendment gives 24 months (from 30.01.2026) to make the IFSC appointment, with regulated India/foreign custodians permitted in the interim. | PLAIN Onshoring custody to GIFT City, with a realistic transition. The local-law carve-out follows mandatory foreign rules, with information arrangements for IFSCA. | WATCH The old Explanation II was substituted — if your compliance calendar still shows the pre-2026 transition, it’s wrong. || Valuation: named independents, one schedule: LAW Assets valued per Sixth Schedule norms by an independent service provider: fund administrator, custodian, Authority-registered credit rating agency, or IBBI-registered valuer. FoF look-through exemption applies. | PLAIN Not "any independent person" — a closed list of four professional categories. Norms in the Sixth Schedule; execution by the named independents; obligation shared by FME and fiduciaries. | WATCH "Any SEBI-registered merchant banker" or "any CA" are not on the list — favourite wrong options. || The reporting clock: LAW Annual report to the Authority AND abridged summary to investors within 4 months of FY-end; full report within 15 days of an investor request. Auditor must be "not in any way associated" with the FME. Monthly holding statements; 10 working days for ad hoc requests. | PLAIN One 4-month clock for both audiences, an auditor test stricter than mere independence, and a monthly transparency baseline. | WATCH "Not in any way associated" closes side-relationship loopholes that ordinary independence tests miss.
lessons.tip: Put the three custody triggers on your AUM dashboard — retail, open-ended, USD 70M — and diarise the 24-month IFSC-custodian runway from 30.01.2026. Amendment deadlines don’t send reminders; your calendar is the control.

lessons.title: Learn the concepts
lessons.hook: A departing director asks for a liability release letter — "standard practice, just sign it." Do you?
lessons.cards: Fiduciaries — the second line: LAW Before filing any scheme: fiduciaries appointed by form — Board of Directors (company), Designated Partners (LLP), Trustees (trust). All fit and proper; retail fiduciaries need prior Authority approval; duties per Third Schedule Part B. | PLAIN Every scheme gets a supervisory layer matched to its legal form, bound by its own code of conduct. | WATCH Part A of the Third Schedule is the FME’s code; Part B is the fiduciaries’. Two codes, one schedule. || The CEO cannot delegate the buck: LAW Under the Code of Conduct, the CEO (whatever the designation) ensures regulatory compliance, that investments serve unit holders’ interests, and owns the overall risk management function. | PLAIN Internal delegation reorganises work, never accountability. The Code names the CEO personally. | WATCH Liability for acts in office SURVIVES termination and cannot be contracted away — no agreement, indemnity or resignation letter erases it. The FME also answers for its employees’ acts. || Committees, fees, ads and mergers: LAW Investment Committee: optional — but members inherit FME/fund-manager responsibilities. Fees: identified and appropriated separately PER SCHEME, each expense a line item with maximums in the offer document. Advertisements: Fifth Schedule code. Scheme mergers/demergers: Authority conditions + prior approval. | PLAIN Four governance disciplines with one theme: nothing pooled, nothing vague, nothing restructured without the regulator. | WATCH Joining the IC is joining the liability — the committee is a brain, never a shield. And investor consent alone cannot merge schemes.
lessons.tip: Minute Investment Committee decisions as if members were KMPs — regulatorily, they carry FME responsibilities. Attendance, dissent and rationale should read like board minutes, not informal notes: the IC is a brain, never a shield.

lessons.title: Learn the concepts
lessons.hook: Tuesday, 9:12 AM: IFSCA appoints an Inspecting Authority for GreenGate. No allegation stated. A director asks: "Can they even do that?"
lessons.cards: Transparency on a monthly clock: LAW Investors get holding statements at the end of every month, and within 10 working days on request. Fiduciaries must disclose anything with an adverse bearing on investments. | PLAIN The baseline rhythm of investor communication — monthly by default, 10 working days on demand, and bad news travels without being asked. | WATCH MONTHLY holdings vs ANNUAL reports (4 months, Module 9) — two different clocks, commonly swapped in questions. || Inspection — no trigger needed: LAW The Authority may appoint an Inspecting Authority suo motu, or on information or complaint, at ANY time — covering books, records, documents, infrastructure, procedures, systems, and associated entities. Everyone — PO, partners, trustees, directors, KMPs, employees, agents — must assist and give reasonable premises access. | PLAIN Inspection is not an event that requires cause; it’s a standing possibility. The cooperation duty reaches every human connected to the FME, down to agents. | WATCH "Only after a show-cause notice" is wrong; "only the compliance officer must cooperate" is wrong. No trigger, no narrow net. || Winding up — three roads and a regulator’s hammer: LAW Grounds: tenure over; 75% of investors by value resolve; or (post-2026) funds raised but minimum corpus missed within the extended validity and the FME opts to wind up voluntarily. The Authority may also DIRECT winding up, merge schemes, or hand an FME’s schemes to ANOTHER FME to manage. | PLAIN Exit is as regulated as entry. The 2026 ground gives failed raises a clean statutory door. And the directive power to transplant scheme management is IFSC’s resolution mechanism for failing managers. | WATCH The investor vote is 75% by value — the same supermajority you’ve now seen in three modules. Retail extensions used 2/3; winding up uses 75%. Keep the fractions apart.
lessons.tip: Maintain a standing inspection-ready index: monthly investor statements, annual reports, fee schedules, custody and valuation agreements, KMP files. Producing documents within the Inspecting Authority’s timeline is itself a Reg. 139 obligation — the index is how you meet it calmly.

lessons.title: Learn the concepts
lessons.hook: The Gazette drops an amendment at 6 PM. The board meets at 9 AM. What do they actually need from you?
lessons.cards: July 2025 — third-party fund management arrives: LAW Part D (Reg. 107A–107D): an FME may manage schemes of third parties, with Authority authorisation; the arrangement must be in company/LLP form; and the FME’s liability is NON-DELEGABLE notwithstanding any indemnity. | PLAIN A new business line with an old principle bolted on: you can outsource the work, never the responsibility. | WATCH "Notwithstanding any indemnity" — the contract can shift money, not accountability. || January 2026 — the KMP rebuild: LAW Reg. 7’s KMP clause (b) substituted: an eligible-institution framework with a 5-year base experience route, 3 years with a professional qualification, and 2/3-year certification routes. | PLAIN The talent gate widened — professional qualifications and certifications now buy down the experience requirement. | WATCH The routes differ by which KMP and which sub-regulation — precision matters more here than anywhere. || January 2026 — the extension revolution: LAW Reg. 19(3) and 35(2): MULTIPLE 6-month PPM extensions, applied for while the PPM is still valid — 25% of the fresh-scheme fee for the first, 50% for each subsequent. Reg. 55(3) for SSFs: UNTOUCHED (one-time, 6 months, 50%). | PLAIN The single most examined change of the year — and its power comes from the asymmetry: everyone upgraded except the SSF. | WATCH File WHILE VALID. A lapsed PPM cannot be revived by an extension application — the timing condition is part of the rule. || January 2026 — gates, exits and custody clocks: LAW New proviso to Reg. 35(1): open-ended schemes touch unlisted securities only after achieving USD 3M corpus. New Reg. 131(1)(c): voluntary winding-up where the (extended) raise still misses minimum corpus. Reg. 132 Expl. II substituted: 24 months from 30.01.2026 to appoint the IFSC custodian, regulated interim custody permitted. | PLAIN Three moving parts of one design: a protective gate while schemes are small, a clean exit when raises fail, and a realistic runway for onshoring custody. | WATCH Each of these starts a CLOCK or sets a GATE — amendment mastery means knowing the dates, not just the rules.
lessons.tip: Convert every amendment into three lists within 24 hours: GATES (what’s now blocked), CLOCKS (deadlines that just started), OPTIONS (routes now open). File the memo — contemporaneous amendment-response evidence is the strongest good-faith document a fund house can show.

lessons.source: 29th IFSCA Authority Meeting, 24 July 2026 (approved; not yet notified)
lessons.title: Learn the concepts
lessons.hook: The board reads that IFSCA has approved a 25% FME contribution ceiling, and wants to commit 18% of the new VC scheme's corpus next week. Do you clear it?
lessons.cards: “Approved” is not “notified”: LAW At its 29th meeting on 24 July 2026, the Authority approved a set of amendments to the IFSCA (Fund Management) Regulations, 2025 aimed at ease of doing business, greater disclosure and regulatory clarity. | PLAIN Approval is the decision to amend. The binding text arrives only when the amendment is notified in the Gazette. Until then, the 2025 Regulations as amended to 30 January 2026 remain the operative law — every drill in Modules 1–12 still states the law that binds you today. | WATCH Two opposite errors are possible. Acting on an unnotified change is a breach. Ignoring it in your planning is poor advice. A compliance officer tracks both columns. || The contribution ceiling moves 10% → 25%: LAW In place of the existing 10% limit, FMEs and their associates having Indian ultimate beneficial owners will be permitted to contribute up to 25% of the corpus of VC Schemes and Restricted Schemes, where such schemes invest only in IFSC or foreign jurisdictions. | PLAIN Headroom for Indian-owned managers building an overseas track record. The floors (2.5% / 5% / USD 750K / USD 1.5M) are untouched — this raises the ceiling only, and only for a defined set. | WATCH It is conditional, not general: Indian UBO AND the scheme invests only in IFSC/foreign jurisdictions. Do not confuse it with the ceiling carve-out ALREADY in force under Reg. 28(1)/40 for FMEs resident outside India with no Indian UBO and not more than one-third of corpus in one investee. || Timelines and valuation relax: LAW The scheme Annual Report timeline extends from four (4) to six (6) months from financial year end. Close-ended Restricted Schemes may move NAV computation and disclosure from semi-annual to annual, subject to prior approval of at least 75% of investors by value. Independent valuation is relaxed for investments in underlying scheme(s) already valued by an independent entity. | PLAIN Three operational easements. Note the middle one is not automatic — it is unlocked by an investor supermajority, the framework's recurring 75%-by-value lever. | WATCH Until notified, Reg. 134's four-month clock governs. Diarise four months; plan for six. || New structures: blended finance: LAW VC Schemes and Restricted Schemes will be permitted to issue multiple classes of units with differential distribution rights — junior / subordinate classes may carry returns lower than, or bear losses higher than, their entitlement. Minimum investment in junior classes: USD 1 Million from non-individual Accredited Investors, or USD 2 Million from other investors. An ESG Scheme may accept funds as grants, subject to conditions. | PLAIN An enabling provision for blended finance — concessional or first-loss capital sitting beneath commercial capital to mobilise private money into climate and development projects. | WATCH The PPM must adequately and prominently disclose the classes, their distribution rights and the resulting risks; the FME and its KMPs must diligence compliance with Indian law and other Indian regulators. || Investor protection tightens in parallel: LAW Retail offer-document disclosures expand to cover NAV computation methodology and conflicts of interest. Internal policies required under the regulations must be approved by the FME's governing body (or its delegate). Temporary deployment of monies before a scheme reaches minimum corpus will be permitted only in capital-preservation and liquidity instruments, with prior PPM/offer-document disclosure. The definition of “associate” expands to reach natural persons and non-body-corporate juridical persons holding a direct economic interest. | PLAIN Ease of business is paired with sharper governance. The wider “associate” definition matters most — it widens every conflict test that keys off that term. | WATCH A broader “associate” means transactions that pass your conflict screen today may need 75%-by-value investor approval once notified. Re-run the screen when it lands. || Also approved — beyond the FM Regulations: LAW The Authority also approved an amendment to the IFSCA (Capital Market Intermediaries) Regulations, 2025 on withdrawal of credit ratings by CRAs; the IFSCA (Prohibition of Market Abuse in Securities Markets) Regulations, 2026; and the IFSCA (Electronic Trading Platform) Regulations, 2026. | PLAIN The market-abuse framework is the one to watch from a fund seat: a unified regime prohibiting insider trading and fraudulent, manipulative and unfair trade practices across the IFSC securities market. | WATCH It is a separate regulation, not an FM Regulations amendment — but it will bind your dealing desk and your personal-trading policy all the same.
lessons.tip: Keep a two-column register: GAZETTED (binds today) and APPROVED (design for it). Put the gazette status on every line of every board paper. That one habit prevents both premature compliance and a late scramble — and it is the cheapest good-faith evidence you can show a supervisor.
